notes: Full Court of Appeal judgment on late amendment withdrawing contractual admissions.

enrichment.short_title: Late defence amendment after admitting direct contract causes irremediable prejudice
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Cluley sued heating contractor RL Dix for defective Nu-Heat underfloor heating at their Worcestershire home; Dix admitted a direct contractual relationship and warranties in its Defence.
Dix later sought permission to amend to deny any direct contract with the Cluleys, relying on the main building contract with Churchill Builders as main contractor.
Churchill was struck off in October 2002 and limitation against Churchill and the architect had expired or was about to expire by the time amendment was permitted in June 2003.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claimants' appeal against HHJ Kirkham's grant of permission to Dix and Nu-Heat to amend pleadings to withdraw admissions on contractual nexus.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; judge's order set aside; permission to amend refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where a defendant has admitted a direct contractual relationship and only belatedly seeks to withdraw that admission, causing prejudice that cannot be compensated in costs because the claimant can no longer join alternative defendants within limitation, the court should refuse the amendment; it is not open to a claimant who sued on the basis of an admission to be treated as having failed to identify proper targets for the claim.
legal_issues: Whether permission to amend a defence to withdraw admissions should be refused for irremediable prejudice
Whether claimants were authors of their own misfortune by not joining Churchill or the architect earlier
Application of the overriding objective and Ketteman principles to late procedural changes

notes: CCRC reference on mandatory life sentence following Offen.

enrichment.short_title: Mandatory life sentence quashed where judge ignored Offen exceptional circumstances
key_facts: Mark Samuel Jackson was convicted of causing grievous bodily harm with intent after striking a man with a hammer following a road altercation; breath alcohol was not involved.
He had prior convictions for attempted robbery and firearms offences, triggering the mandatory life sentence regime for second serious offences.
The sentencing judge and defence counsel treated life imprisonment as inevitable without analysing exceptional circumstances or risk to the public.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against sentence on reference by the Criminal Cases Review Commission under section 9 of the Criminal Appeal Act 1995.
enrichment.outcome: Life sentence quashed; substituted six years' imprisonment for the GBH offence plus twelve months consecutive for breach of licence (seven years total from original sentence date).
enrichment.ratio: A judge imposing a mandatory life sentence under section 2 of the Crime Sentences Act 1997 must consider whether exceptional circumstances exist and whether the offender poses a significant risk to the public as clarified in R v Offen; on a CCRC reference, later psychiatric and prison reports may be applied retrospectively to assess the risk that should have been considered at sentence (following Watkins).
legal_issues: Whether the judge failed to consider exceptional circumstances under section 2
Whether risk to the public must be assessed at the time of sentence
Whether post-sentence psychiatric evidence may be relied on on appeal

notes: Judicial review declarations on Schedule 3 deposition procedure.

enrichment.short_title: Schedule 3 depositions must be in open court; self-incrimination claims require investigation
key_facts: In a murder prosecution, witness CB was summonsed under Schedule 3 para 4 to give a deposition but refused further questions on legal advice that answers might incriminate her.
Bolton justices treated the procedure as not sitting in open court and excluded police officers; they accepted solicitor advice as sufficient just excuse without investigating each question.
The court granted declarations on amended judicial review grounds rather than quashing a decision never formally made on open court.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim for judicial review of Bolton Magistrates' Court decisions on Schedule 3 deposition procedure; leave granted to amend for declaratory relief.
enrichment.outcome: Declarations made that Schedule 3 para 4 depositions are proceedings in open court (subject to exceptional exclusion) and that each self-incrimination claim must be properly investigated by the justices; irregular deposition may be retaken.
enrichment.ratio: Proceedings under paragraph 4 of Schedule 3 to the Crime and Disorder Act 1998 are normally proceedings in open court, including the party seeking the deposition and investigating officers; a witness's claim of privilege against self-incrimination must be investigated by the justices in respect of each question and cannot be delegated to the witness's solicitor's advice.
legal_issues: Whether Schedule 3 para 4 deposition procedure is a proceeding in open court
Whether justices may exclude police officers and CPS representatives
Whether legal advice that answers may incriminate constitutes just excuse without judicial investigation

notes: Short case stated on burglary joint enterprise.

enrichment.short_title: Knowing others are burgling and remaining outside is not burglary
key_facts: The appellant was charged jointly with two others with burglary of Jarvis Workspace commercial premises.
Youth court found he did not know the others' plan initially, warned them they were committing burglary, followed them back but remained outside while knowing their purpose.
No finding that he acted as lookout, assisted, or encouraged the burglary.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Defendant's appeal by way of case stated from Bridlington Youth Court conviction for burglary.
enrichment.ratio: On findings that a defendant merely knew co-defendants were burgling premises and chose to remain outside, without assisting, encouraging, or acting as lookout, those facts without more are insufficient to establish either the actus reus or mens rea of burglary or joint enterprise liability.
legal_issues: Whether knowledge of others' burglary plus presence outside constitutes burglary
Whether joint enterprise requires assistance or encouragement beyond mere presence

notes: Section 288 planning appeal; truncated summary in source but full judgment present.

enrichment.short_title: Gypsy site inspector failed to consider individual plot permissions separately
key_facts: Eight gypsy appellants jointly bought a field near Swavesey and applied for permission for mobile homes and caravans on individual plots; they occupied unlawfully from September 2002.
The Inspector refused all eight appeals chiefly because total numbers (up to 32 caravans and eight mobile homes) would dominate the rural landscape.
She considered personal circumstances globally rather than whether some individual appellants with compelling needs (children's education, elderly care) might be granted permission.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 288 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 against Inspector's dismissal of eight planning appeals; linked enforcement and judicial review proceedings stayed.
enrichment.outcome: Decision quashed and remitted to the Secretary of State; claimants awarded 75% of costs; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where multiple gypsy site applications are heard together, an inspector who refuses all appeals primarily because aggregate caravan numbers harm landscape character must still consider whether personal circumstances justify granting permission to some individual appellants rather than treating the site only as a global encampment; failure to do so renders the decision flawed.
legal_issues: Whether the Inspector failed to consider national gypsy site need as a material consideration
Whether a condition limiting caravan numbers should have been considered
Whether individual personal circumstances were adequately weighed against global landscape impact
Article 8 and education rights arguments

notes: Special reasons appeal on unknowing consumption of alcoholic punch.

enrichment.short_title: Driver must inquire about punch contents; no special reasons without enquiry
key_facts: The appellant, a Rastafarian who avoided alcohol for seven years, drank two glasses at a funeral believing they were fruit juice; the punch was about 28% alcohol.
He drove shortly afterwards and provided a breath specimen of 83 micrograms (limit 35); magistrates found him credible but held he made no enquiries about the drink's contents.
He had prior drink-driving conviction and knew the taste of alcohol from before becoming Rastafarian.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Defendant's appeal by way of case stated against magistrates' refusal to find special reasons for non-disqualification after drink-driving conviction.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; magistrates correctly found no special reasons; costs to prosecution.
enrichment.ratio: A driver at a party where alcohol is served who assumes without enquiry that a drink is alcohol-free takes the risk of exceeding the limit; ignorance of alcohol content without enquiry cannot amount to special reasons, unlike laced-drink cases where a third party intervenes without the driver's knowledge; the driver must do all reasonably expected to avoid the offence.
legal_issues: Whether there is a positive duty to inquire about drink contents before driving
Whether unknowing consumption of alcoholic punch can be special reasons
Distinction from laced-drink authorities

enrichment.short_title: Severe motorcycle injury awards upheld on PSLA, earnings, home and prostheses
key_facts: David Pinnington suffered catastrophic injuries in a July 1998 motorcycle accident including amputation of his dominant right arm, left wrist damage, hip and knee injuries, and cognitive/psychological effects; liability was admitted.

Judge Bursell awarded £1,171,719.52 including £145,000 general damages, nil residual earning capacity, £39,936 future accommodation costs, and £215,900 for prostheses (later agreed reduction to £181,400 on double-counting).
Crossleigh Construction appealed four heads; the Court of Appeal refused to interfere with jury-type awards on each.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Defendant's appeal with permission on general damages, residual earning capacity, accommodation, and prostheses costs following High Court assessment of damages.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on all grounds; defendants' costs on indemnity basis after Part 36 offer.
enrichment.ratio: The Court of Appeal will not interfere with a trial judge's assessment of personal injury damages unless manifestly excessive; awards for general damages reflecting multiple severe injuries, nil residual earning capacity where rehabilitation evidence showed no measurable employment chance, reasonable accommodation needs, and private prostheses where NHS provision was not locally available were within the judge's proper discretion.

Whether nil award for residual earning capacity was wrong in principle
Whether future accommodation costs based on current rented bungalow were reasonable necessity
Whether private prostheses costs were recoverable under Woodrup v Nichol principles

notes: Attorney General unduly lenient sentence reference.

enrichment.short_title: Two-day robbery spree sentence increased from 3½ years to five years
key_facts: Leon Mark Jameson, aged 21, pleaded guilty to eight offences over two days in March 2003 including theft of cars used to facilitate shop robberies and an attempted handbag snatch while cycling victim was dragged alongside a moving car.
He was on an 18-month Community Rehabilitation Order imposed only three months earlier and had a bad record of theft and short custodial sentences.
Recorder Bond imposed 30 months consecutive on first robbery plus concurrent sentences totalling 3½ years including resentenced breach matters.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 alleging unduly lenient sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Reference allowed; total sentence increased to five years' imprisonment by substituting four years consecutive on attempted robbery count 6.
enrichment.ratio: A concerted short crime spree involving stolen vehicles, multiple shop robberies targeting vulnerable premises, a dangerous attempted robbery dragging a cyclist, breach of a recent CRO, and a bad criminal record warranted a substantially higher total sentence than that appropriate for a single robbery; attempted robbery count merited four years consecutive subject to totality and double jeopardy.
legal_issues: Whether total sentence reflected gravity of concerted criminality
Appropriate sentence for attempted robbery dragging cyclist alongside car
Whether CRO breach sentence should run consecutively
Application of Attorney General's reference sentencing guidelines

notes: DPP appeal on aggravated trespass and defence of property at GM crop site.

enrichment.short_title: GM crop protesters cannot rely on defence of property against lawful drilling

statutes_considered.statute: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: Four protesters attached themselves to tractors drilling GM and non-GM maize at Horselynch Plantation, Weymouth, on Michael Jones's private farmland under government trial consents.
They trespassed and intended to disrupt lawful planting; they honestly believed GM crops threatened neighbouring property via pollen and soil transfer but knew the drilling was not unlawful.
District Judge acquitted on the basis their actions were reasonable defence of property; DPP appealed by case stated.
enrichment.procedural_posture: DPP appeal by way of case stated from Sherborne Magistrates' Court acquittal for aggravated trespass.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; case remitted with direction to convict; respondents to pay DPP's costs in this court.
enrichment.ratio: The common law defence of property by proportionate force requires that the defendant believed unlawful or criminal damage to property was being or was about to be inflicted; it is not available where the lawful activity protested (here licensed GM maize drilling) is not unlawful, even if protesters honestly fear environmental harm; the Criminal Damage Act lawful excuse scheme is distinct and broader.
legal_issues: Whether defence of property is available against aggravated trespass at lawful GM crop trial
Whether protesters' honest beliefs about environmental harm provide lawful justification
Distinction between common law defence of property and Criminal Damage Act section 5(2)(b)
